# How to Write a Calm, Polite Message to a Neighbor With Lumo

> **In short:** You will describe a problem to Lumo, get a friendly draft, and edit it so it sounds like you. Lumo helps you write, but you send the message yourself. Lumo's help center says your chats are stored with zero-access encryption, so Proton cannot read them.

Sometimes a neighbor's late-night party keeps you awake, and you want to speak up without starting a feud. Writing that first message is the hard part. This guide is for anyone who has never used Lumo before. By the end, you will have a polite, calm message ready to send, written in your own voice.

## Before you start

- **A Proton Account.** Lumo's help center explains that you reach your chats by logging in to your Proton Account, so have your login details ready.
- **Access to Lumo.** Open Lumo the way you normally open Proton's services. The official help center at proton.me/support has the current details.
- **About 15 minutes.** The whole process usually takes less than that once you are signed in.
- **Your message channel.** Know whether you will send the note by a note under the door, a text, or a call. You will need this in the last step.

## Step 1 — Sign in to your Proton Account

Start by logging in to your Proton Account with your email address and password. Lumo's help center says your chats are tied to this account, so signing in is what lets you reach your conversation history. Once you are logged in, you should be able to get to Lumo from Proton's services. The exact route can change, so if you don't see a Lumo option right away, look for a link or menu item that mentions Lumo, or check the official help center.

If you have two-step verification turned on, you may need a code from your phone or another approved method. That is normal and works the same way it does for any sign-in.

💬 Example: No text is needed for this step. Just sign in with your usual details.

You'll know it worked when you are logged in and can open a screen where you can type a message to Lumo.

## Step 2 — Open a new chat and describe the situation

Open a new chat so you start with a clean conversation. You should see an empty area with a message box, usually near the bottom of the screen. Click or tap in the message box and type out what is happening. Use your own words and keep the facts simple: the day, the time, and what you heard. You do not need to be polite in this message, because Lumo is only drafting for you.

Including the facts helps Lumo write something specific instead of a vague note. Lumo's help center says it can help you write messages, so describing the situation clearly is the right kind of request. If your first message is very short, Lumo may ask a question or give you something general, and that is fine.

💬 Example: "My neighbor [neighbor's first name] had a loud party last Saturday that went past midnight. I'm a light sleeper and have a work shift early on Mondays. I'd like to ask them to keep noise down later on weekend nights."

You'll know it worked when Lumo's reply appears below your message and mentions the party or the late hour.

## Step 3 — Ask for a friendly draft

Now tell Lumo exactly what kind of message you want. Name the tone you are aiming for and the length you need. A short, warm note usually works better for a first conversation than a long letter. Ask Lumo to avoid blame and to focus on how you feel and what you need. Make it clear that this is a first message, not a complaint to a landlord or an official notice.

If the answer is too stiff, too long, or sounds like a lecture, don't worry. You can ask for changes in the same chat, and Lumo will adjust the draft based on what you tell it. Keep your requests simple, one change at a time.

💬 Example: "Please write a calm, friendly note I can leave for a neighbor. It should be under 80 words, sound polite but not formal, and avoid blaming them. End with a line thanking them for their understanding."

You'll know it worked when you get a complete draft you could read out loud without cringing.

## Step 4 — Edit the draft until it sounds like you

Read the draft out loud, slowly. Change any word you would never say, such as a phrase that sounds too fancy, and cut any sentence that feels like a threat. Add a detail only you would know, like a shared fence or the name of the street you live on. The best version is the one that sounds natural when you speak it.

If you want a different approach, you can ask Lumo for a softer version or a shorter one in the same chat. Compare the options and keep the parts you like. Lumo's suggestions are a starting point, and the final words should be yours.

💬 Example: "Make this sound more casual, as if I'm talking to a neighbor I've waved to before. Keep the request about quieter weekend nights."

You'll know it worked when the message reads like something you would actually say to the person.

## Step 5 — Copy the message and send it yourself

Select the final text and copy it. Then paste it into the channel you chose earlier, such as a note, a text, or an email if you have their address. Lumo does not send messages on your behalf, as far as its help center describes. Its job is to help you write, so the sending step is yours.

Before you send, check the names, the time, and any detail you added. A small mistake in a name can make a friendly note look careless. Once it is sent, you can follow up in person if the problem continues.

💬 Example: Paste your final draft into your text app and add your neighbor's name at the top before you send.

You'll know it worked when the message is sent through your chosen channel and you have a copy saved for your records.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending the first draft without reading it.** Drafts often sound a little generic. Fix this by reading it aloud and changing any phrase that does not sound like you.
- **Leaving out the facts.** A vague request like "be quiet" can feel harsh. Fix this by naming the day, the time, and the reason the noise matters to you.
- **Sharing private details with more than you need to.** Your message only needs what is relevant. Fix this by keeping the note short and focused on the situation.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** You can draft calm notes for any small neighborly issue, like a parking spot, a shared trash bin, or a dog that barks at dawn.
- **For your business or work:** You can use the same approach to draft polite follow-up emails to a coworker or a client, then edit them to match your relationship with them.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with one low-stakes message you have been putting off. A short draft is enough to show you how the process feels.

## Try it now

Open a new chat in Lumo and type one sentence describing a small, real situation you need to address. Then ask for a polite, short draft. You don't have to send it. Just see how it sounds, and make one edit so it feels like yours.
